        HEN I WROTE THE book Building Small Boilers for Gas Firing
           in 2013, each of the four larger boilers, the three vertical
          fire-tube ones, and the horizontal water-tube one, wasW
fitted with a commercially available ceramic burner. These burners
were either round or rectangular and worked extremely well. They
were also quite expensive to purchase.
   This led me to wonder whether I could make my own burners
with similar dimensions. I discovered that the jewellery trade uses
ceramic honeycomb for manufacturing decorative items. This
honeycomb material is hard, resists crumbling, and has proved to be
ideal for making ceramic burners. Furthermore, the plumbing trade
provides a large variety of end caps that are suitable for use as
housings for all the circular burners, together with the occasional
length of copper tube. All the burners need short lengths of brass rod
for the gas-jet holders and housings, and the rectangular burners
require small flat sheets of copper or brass, widely available from the
suppliers to model engineers. The success of these designs led to
the production of some even smaller burners, suitable for Mamod,
Wilesco and similar-size small boilers.
     I must thank my friend Kevin Walton, who has provided much of
the technical input and detailed recommendations that have made
possible the building of the burners described in this book. He has
also helped with the construction of all the burners, and has solved

some significant problems relating to how they were built and in their
operation.
    Finally, I must mention my appreciation of my wife Lynda, who
has had to put up with all the work involved in making the burners,
testing and photographing them, as well as the many months writing
up and organizing the results on my computer.

Introduction




       EAT HAS ALWAYS BEEN an essential for humans. Its earliest use
     was in the form of wood fires used to keep warm and to cook
       food. For some people, oil or tar emerged from the surface ofH
the ground and was also found to burn well. It was particularly useful
for providing torchlight at night. The first steam-powered device
dates back to ancient Greek times, but it wasn’t until the start of the
industrial revolution that useful work was obtained from steam
engines.
   There is something incredibly appealing about operating model
steam engines. They may require a heat source and a boiler to
generate the steam, but they produce almost silent power, normally
without the need for gear changes to drive their load. And they are a
glorious reminder of the golden age of the industrial revolution.
   Steam engines, as originally envisaged by Newcomen, Trevithick,
Watt and others, have become the life blood of many preservation
organizations, but the steam turbine, invented by Charles Parsons, is
still happily turning the generators in power stations that produce
electricity, as well as propellers in some ships. The steam generators
for these turbines may be heated by coal, gas, oil or a controlled
nuclear chain reaction.

FIG. 1
A Stuart beam engine powered by a 108mm (41⁄4in) vertical fire-tube boiler heated by a
                   67mm round ceramic burner.

FIG. 2
  A 76mm (3in) horizontal water-tube boiler fitted with a 70 × 50mm rectangular burner
                       steaming a single-cylinder mill engine.

   Running a model steam engine on compressed air is neither
good for the engine nor in any sense realistic. Running on steam
from the right size of model boiler is exhilarating, and with a
displacement lubricator, feeds small amounts of oil through the
valves into the cylinder to minimize wear to the valve gear and on
the cylinder/piston combination.
   There are many ways of heating the water in a model steam
boiler. They include using coal, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG),
paraffin, methylated spirits, impregnated pellets and historically
petrol, although petrol is not considered a safe option in the twenty-
first century. This is because petrol vapour is explosive, and as a

result, using a petrolfuelled blowlamp to heat a boiler has,
fortunately, all but disappeared.
   Each source of heat comes with its own set of problems. With
coal, the fire requires a stoker, normally human, to add coal regularly
to the firebox. Starting the fire with kindling can also be a time-
consuming task. On the other hand, LPG gives a virtually
instantaneous heat and can provide a high heat output. However, it
does require a safe gas tank and care in handling the gas. Paraffin
or kerosene is not a very volatile liquid and is difficult to vaporize
ready for burning. Methylated spirits will produce relatively small
amounts of heat, and again will require a safe spirit container. The
flame is virtually invisible and the storage tank must be protected
from the heat.
   However, neither methylated spirits nor LPG need an operator in
attendance. They are thus suitable for installation in model vehicles
and steam boats – but take care to ensure the heat source is
exhausted before the boiler water has run out. The same warning
applies to stationary installations. A boiler that has run out of water is
readily destroyed if the heating is not turned off.
   Over the past ten years, the author and Kevin Walton have
designed and built nine different boilers of a variety of shapes, sizes
and configurations, but all within the 3-bar litre limit detailed in the
UK Boiler Test Code 2018 Volume 2. Some years ago Building Small
Boilers for Gas Firing was published by Camden Miniature Steam
Services, giving detailed instructions on how to build these boilers.
The majority of the boilers were heated by commercial ceramic
burners, but some subsequent experiments led to fitting new home-
made burners to most of these boilers, and writing about how to
make the burners in a typical model engineer’s workshop, and also
how to operate these burners.
   As a result, this book describes a range of easy-tomake ceramic
burners for the home builder. They all burn a propane/butane gas

mixture, two of a range of LPGs that are widely available. These
burners provide high heat outputs from burners of relatively small
size, are clean to operate, and that may be powered from small
disposable gas cylinders or from easy-to-purchase refillable ones.
However, do take care when using these gases. They are heavier
(denser) than air and will therefore pool in any enclosed area – the
floor of a workshop, the hull of a model boat or even the interior of a
car. With air they form a volatile mixture that can readily be ignited by
either a spark or a naked flame. While this sounds a very severe
area for concern, provided you are careful, their use as a fuel
presents no problems, and it is worth remembering that they are
widely used for camping stoves.
   There are several different commercially available designs of
small burner for model steam boilers currently on the market. Some
use a ceramic element, and there are several different types of
ceramic element, while some use a metal disc with holes drilled in it.
Of burners that plug into a horizontal flue, some have secondary air
holes, some do not. The same is true of the similarly configured
burners described in this book. All the burners described in this
volume use a hard ceramic element of the type used by the jewellery
trade, rather than the softer type that is more prone to damage.

FIG. 3
An 89mm (31⁄2in) vertical fire-tube boiler heated by a 54mm round burner.

FIG. 4
           Construction details are given for all eleven of these ceramic burners.

   Three different configurations and nine different sizes of burner
are described in detail in this book, together with two minor variants.
They are shown in Figure 4. They are all suitable for use in boilers

that are below the 3-bar litre limit covered in the UK Boiler Test Code
2018. Such boilers face a less stringent testing regime than larger
boilers. Three different-size burners are suitable for fitting in the
centre flues of boilers, and there is one variant for any boiler where
the end of the flue is flush with the boiler end plate. The other six
burners fit in a firebox and are suited to heating vertical fire-tube or
horizontal water-tube boilers, or even just pot boilers. There are
three different sizes of round burner, and likewise three rectangular
ones, again with a variant made from brass sheet instead of copper.
   The nine larger designs work well, are quick to build, and
maintain steam pressure in suitably sized boilers, typically vertical
ones varying in size from 51mm (2in) to 108mm (41⁄4in) diameter.
Horizontal boilers with 28mm, 35mm or 42mm flues should not
exceed 108mm (41⁄4in) diameter or 250mm (10in) long. The same
size limitations apply to horizontal boilers with a firebox below.

FIG. 5
This Mamod traction engine will run well with a small round burner fitted in the firebox.

FIG. 6
A squat 108mm (41⁄4in) boat boiler with a 67mm round ceramic burner on a test rig
                  steaming a twin-cylinder Marcher engine.

FIG. 7
The Stuart 4000 boiler running at 30psi (2 bar) with a 42mm burner and brass adapter ring,
  driving a Stuart Double 10 engine turning a small generator powering the overhead light.

   The two smallest burners, one round and one rectangular, also
perform extremely well and have been specially designed to heat the

boilers of Mamod, Wilesco and similar static steam plants, as well as
their steam rollers and traction engines such as the one in Figure 5.
    All burners require both primary and secondary sources of air if
the gas is to burn efficiently. Primary air passes through holes drilled
in the gas-jet housings of all the burners, and the jet can be moved
by undoing the locking bolt in its holder and moving the jet further in
or out of the housing. For the two larger burners that fit in flues, the
secondary air comes with the primary air, while the holes in the outer
shell of the two smallest burners provide secondary air. All the
vertically mounted burners draw their air through holes in the boiler
firebox.

FIG. 8
The 67mm round burner is well alight and showing blue cones.

FIG. 9
The large rectangular burner provides plenty of heat and is burning well.

FIG. 10
The smallest rectangular burner provides excellent heat for its size, and has blue cones
                          visible on the top of its ceramic element.

FIG. 11
  The 42mm burner well alight with the jet correctly adjusted to provide a good hot flame.

   To make any of these burners some fairly basic skills in drilling,
tapping and turning will be required. The small number of parts that
will be needed can be made using a lathe, but for the smallest 28mm

burner you will really need access to a milling machine and a rotary
table. For all the burners, you will also need to gain the ability to
carry out simple silver soldering, a skill that many model engineers
have already learned. This can be done with a relatively small, self-
contained MAP (methylacetylenepropadiene) torch or a larger
propane gas torch with a modest-size head. Some firebricks, heat-
resisting blocks or Vermiculite board will also be needed to support
the work being soldered.
   The seven round burners are made using copper plumbing end
caps of the appropriate dimensions. The rectangular ones use folded
copper or brass boxes. The right size gas jet for each particular
burner will be required, and a jet holder with pipe that can be
connected to the valve of a small gas container. These are available
from a number of model engineering suppliers, listed at the end of
this book, or you can turn a holder yourself from brass rod. All the
burners then need a short length of tube turned from brass rod to
provide primary air and to act as a housing for the gas-jet holder.
   The two large round burners and the three larger rectangular
ones need two gas-diffusing components: a short length of stainless-
steel spring of 1⁄2in or 12mm diameter in their bodies from the
primary air tube to the other end of the burner body, and a small strip
of stainless-steel mesh of twenty holes per inch. You will also need a
small block of ceramic material that can be easily cut and filed to
size and shape. The spring, the mesh and the ceramic material can
be glued in place with high-temperature adhesive filler such as
Ceramix, Vitcas or Mapeflex. The smallest rectangular burner needs
a 3⁄8in or 10mm spring and the same mesh.

FIG. 12
 A 35mm burner provides plenty of heat for this 108mm (41⁄4in) horizontal boiler to drive a
                                     Stuart mill engine.

   You may choose to finish copper burners with high-temperature
paint, but this will not work for brass as there are no high-
temperature etch primers. Therefore as an alternative, the burner jet
housings and the brass bodies can be polished.

FIG. 13
The author’s workshop is well equipped with a lathe, milling machine and pillar drill with X/Y
  table. The lathe is the only machine tool necessary for making all but one of the ceramic
                                        burners.

FIG. 14
   Kevin Walton’s workshop also has three similar machine tools, but making the ceramic
                burners has largely been completed on the Chester lathe.

   You may already have a well-equipped workshop such as those
shown in Figures 13 and 14, but as long as you have access to a
lathe, you can make all but one of the burners without any other
workshop machinery.

ABOUT THIS BOOK

Since the main components used to make the burners are metric
sizes, metric dimensions are used but with equivalent imperial
measurements where these are practicable. In some cases, there is
no imperial equivalent. For example, gas pipe connectors require
1⁄8in copper pipe and 3mm pipe would not be suitable. Likewise, gas

jets are threaded 1BA and therefore this imperial thread has to be
used in any gas-jet holder.
   Each chapter commences with a short summary of its contents.
The first chapter starts with an explanation of the various material
and tools, including some basic machine tools that you will need. It is
followed by details of how to silver solder the relatively small burner
bodies and gas pipes. This chapter also includes information on the
types of gas torch you will need for this task, and the LPG they use.
There is then a description of three burners, with one variant, for
boilers with horizontal flues. These burners fit 42mm, 35mm and
28mm flues, but details are given of how to make an adaptor to fit
slightly different-size flues.
   Construction details follow for two round burners, one larger than
the other, for vertical boilers with fireboxes. There are also
instructions on how you can build two different sizes of rectangular
burner for use in horizontal water-tube or pot boilers, with a variant
for the larger one. This is followed by an account of building a small
round and a diminutive oblong burner for use in Mamod and Wilesco
and similar boilers. The next chapter deals with the provision of LPG
for the ceramic burners and the tanks to hold it, as well as the
connecting pipework and necessary valves and connecters.
   Then there is advice on how to set up, install and operate the
burners in your boiler to ensure optimal heating, and for burners that
fit in a firebox, advice on how to avoid blowback and how to repair a
burner if blowback occurs. The following chapter looks at a number
of electronic and mechanical automatic gas-control systems that
monitor the boiler pressure you have set, and adjust the gas flow to
try and maintain the desired pressure. They will help to reduce gas
consumption and simplify the operation of gas-fired boilers in model
boats and land vehicles. This is followed by some conclusions.
    Finally, the Appendix provides a concise summary of the UK
Boiler Test Code 2018 Volume 3 that deals with making LPG tanks

under 250ml capacity. A list of the addresses of useful suppliers
detailing the relevant items they can supply is provided at the end of
this book. There is also a comprehensive index.



  WARNING

   Please ensure that you read and understand the advice on
   using liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) given in Chapters 2 and
   6 before silver soldering any of the gas burners described in
    this book, and before operating them.

1 Materials and Tools


       HIS CHAPTER DESCRIBES ALL the tools and basic ready-made
      items that can be purchased, as well as the raw materials that
        will also be required to build the burners described in thisT
book. It also covers the workshop facilities, including machine tools,
that are likely to be needed. It does not include what is needed for
silver soldering, which is covered in Chapter 2.
   Building ceramic burners is not a difficult task, but does require a
few items not normally found in many modellers’ workshops. One
unusual tool is required, a ceramic saw, as well as high-temperature
adhesive/ filler and high-temperature paint. These are easily
obtained either from DIY or specialist suppliers, or on eBay. Building
burners also requires a range of machine tools, some of which are
fairly normal such as a lathe, and a few that are slightly less
common, but that you may need depending on which burner you
decide to build, such as a vertical milling machine and a rotary table.
Likely to be found in the scrap box are short lengths of brass rod and
possibly some pieces of copper tube.

COPPER AND BRASS

Two metals are predominantly used in the construction of all the
burners in this book: copper and brass. Copper is not simple to
machine or drill but is very malleable and easy to bend into shape.
Drilling is best done with a special copper-drilling bit that looks
similar to a wood drill. Brass, on the other hand, is straightforward to

machine, though drilling can be awkward at the point of
breakthrough. Brass is readily bent but not as easily as copper.
Annealing either metal makes bending relatively simple. Brass needs
an etch primer if you wish to paint it, but to date there are no heat-
resistant etch primers.
     It is important to realize that lengths of copper pipe from plumbing
suppliers will be a different size from those purchased from model
engineering suppliers, so it is important that where end caps and
short lengths of tube are needed, they will fit into each other.

Cutting Lubricant for Copper

A number of lubricants are recommended for use when machining
copper: sulphur-free cutting oil, dry soluble oil, lard oil, and paraffin
or mineral lard oil. A practical tip I learned from Martin Gearing in his
Model Engineer articles on the ME vertical boiler is to use original
bright-green Swarfega Classic as a lubricant when drilling copper. A
can is illustrated in Figure 15. It cleans off easily and has no negative
effect on silver soldering. It is an excellent cutting fluid, or rather a
jelly, for copper. It is still widely available both from Screwfix and
Amazon. For drilling and milling, the bit can be dipped into some
Swarfega, whilst for turning, a brush will prove ideal for applying it.
Although it is also ideal for cleaning hands at the end of a session,
do keep two separate containers to prevent polluting the hand
cleaner with swarf.

FIG. 15
  Swarfega Classic, the original hand cleaner, is a fine lubricant when machining copper.

BURNER BODIES

The bodies of the round burners described in Chapter 3 are made
from copper plumbing end caps of different sizes, and short lengths
of copper plumbing tube. Likewise, all the round burners in Chapters
4 and 5 involve the use of plumbing end caps. A number of different-

size end caps can be seen in Figure 16. It is essential that these end
caps are not the Yorkshire type, as these contain a ring of soft solder
that will make silver soldering impossible. As all copper plumbing
materials are only available in metric dimensions, imperial sizes are
not normally quoted by suppliers.

FIG. 16
  A small selection of copper plumbing end caps, the two left-hand ones for making large
         circular burners, the right-hand pair for making burners to fit horizontal flues.

    All these copper plumbing parts should be to EN 1057 – Type X
(previously BS 2871 Table X). They can be bought from plumbers’
merchants or DIY supermarkets, but it is probably easier and
cheaper to order them on the Internet. For the 28mm burner a pair of

end caps will be needed, one of 22mm and the other of 28mm. The
35mm burner for horizontal flues requires end caps of 28mm and
35mm. Likewise the 42mm burner needs end caps of 35mm and
42mm. In addition, the two larger burners require short lengths of
copper tube, of 28mm and 35mm diameter respectively. You might
have offcuts yourself, or you may be able to scrounge a short length
– 50mm will do – from one of your friends.
     It is possible to build the circular burners for boilers with fireboxes
from 35mm, 54mm or 67mm end caps, depending on the size of
burner required, but the height of the end cap will have to be
reduced: this can be easily done in a lathe or using a hacksaw and
file.

FIG. 17
       The folded copper box that forms the body of the large rectangular burner.

   Any of the larger rectangular burner bodies can be made from
1.6mm thick (16 SWG) copper or brass sheet, cut and folded to size
as illustrated in Figure 17. The smallest oblong one uses 0.9mm (20
SWG) brass sheet. All the oblong burner housings are then silver
soldered at the corners. You will need to drill the bodies, whether
round or square, so that the gas-jet housing you have made can be
silver soldered into place.

GAS-JET HOUSINGS

It is a relatively straightforward task to make the gas-jet housing. Drill
a short length of 1⁄2in or 12mm brass rod right through, and then, for
the smaller burners, turn down one half to a smaller diameter.
Carefully cross-drill the holes for primary air, then drill and tap a
small hole for a 6BA or M3 bolt in order to secure the jet holder in
place and allow its position to be adjusted. Examples of the two main
variants can be seen in Figures 18 and 19.





                                      FIG. 18
       The type of brass gas-jet housings needed for burners for horizontal flues.





                                      FIG. 19
         The different gas-jet housing required for burners that fit in fireboxes.

GAS-JET HOLDERS

While gas-jet holders are widely available from companies that sell
gas jets, they are also very easy to make. All that is needed is a
short length of 8mm (5⁄16in) round brass rod. The holder is 25mm
(1in) long, and is drilled 4.5mm for a depth of 20mm (3⁄4in), and then
tapped 1BA to match the gas jet. Finally, a 1⁄8in hole must be drilled
for the gas pipe. This can be either cross-drilled near the base of the
holder, or through the base depending on how you want the gas pipe
to run.

GAS PIPE

The UK standard for gas pipe, suitable for LPG burners that heat
model boilers, is 1⁄8in. It is normally supplied as bending-grade
copper tube in a coil. The pipe can be easily straightened and cut to
the required length, and then silver soldered into the gas-jet holder.
The other end needs silver soldering into the gas-valve connecter to
the gas tank. A small pipe bender, such as the one shown in Figure
20, will help to ensure a neat installation of the gas pipe.

FIG. 20
A coil of 1⁄8in copper pipe and an economically priced pipe bender to enable the making of a
                              neat gas-pipe installation.

NUT SPINNERS

Adjusting the position of the gas jet in the housing is an awkward
task – holding the housing, moving the gas-jet holder, and loosening
and tightening the bolt that fixes the holder in place in the housing.
Trying to do this using an open-ended spanner is almost impossible,
so the use of a nut spinner makes a difficult task significantly easier.
Figure 21 shows examples of a long and a compact nut spinner used
for this task.

FIG. 21
  Two alternative examples of 6BA nut spinners, either of which will be found useful when
                                     setting up your burner.

GAS-DIFFUSER COMPONENTS

Without any diffusing components, the gas will not be evenly
distributed in the larger burners, and the ceramic material in some of
them will not burn evenly across its surface when lit, seriously
reducing heat output. The burners that plug into the flue have gas-jet
holders that extend to within 3mm (1⁄8in) of the far wall of the burner
body, resulting in the gas dispersing across the relatively small
surface area of the ceramic.
   For the larger round and oblong burners that fit in the firebox,
various possible solutions were tested. These included using a tube
of mesh fitted across the width of the burner body from the gas/air
inlet, a sheet of mesh fitted under the ceramic element, and the use
of baffles in the body of the burner. None of these methods worked
as well as a strip of mesh to diffuse the gas and a length of spring to
give it swirl, which resulted in the gas spreading evenly across the
burner body. The two materials that help resolve this issue, springs
and mesh, are both made of stainless-steel.

Stainless-Steel Springs

The four largest burners have a length of stainlesssteel spring in
their bodies from the gas-jet housing to the other side of the burner
body to impart a degree of swirl to the gas/air mixture entering the
chamber. This can be easily cut from a short length of 1⁄2in or 12mm
diameter stainless-steel spring of 1.6mm thick wire (16 SWG). The
two smallest burners for Mamod and Wilesco boilers use a thinner
3⁄8in (9 or 10mm) diameter stainless-steel spring of 0.9mm (20 SWG)
or 1.2mm (18 SWG) wire thickness. Figure 22 shows examples of
both these springs.

FIG. 22
   Lengths of 3⁄8in (9mm or 10mm) and 1⁄2in or 12mm stainless-steel spring; the former is
    suitable for the smallest oblong burner and the latter for large rectangular and round
                                        burners.

Stainless-Steel Mesh

A small amount of stainless-steel mesh will be needed in the burner
body. This locates where the gas enters the burner body, for all but
one of the burners that fit under the boilers. Twenty holesper-inch

mesh is ideal, so look for the following: 20 mesh – 1.02mm aperture
– 0.25mm wire diameter – SS316L grade – woven wire mesh. An
economic A5 sample sheet is plenty for several burners – a sample
is shown in Figure 23. The mesh is easily cut to size with tin snips or
even old scissors.





                                      FIG. 23
  An A5-size sheet of stainless-steel mesh. Only a small strip is needed for the round or
                         rectangular burners that fit under boilers.

CERAMIC ELEMENTS, AND HOW TO CUT
THEM

The ceramic part of each burner must be cut to shape from a small
sheet of ceramic material, which is widely used in, and is available
from, the jewellery trade. It is a non-asbestos-based material. The
standard thickness is usually 12.5mm (1⁄2in), and this is preferable
for use in burners rather than thicker ceramic honeycomb. It comes
in blocks of about 135 × 95mm (55⁄16 × 3in): such a block can be
seen in Figure 24. Depending on the source of the ceramic, it may
be white or off white, but it always has a pattern on the front with tiny
hills and valleys. As the material is rigid, its reverse side can be
easily marked with a pencil using the burner body as a template.





                                      FIG. 24
  A sheet of the right type of ceramic material for making burners that is used by, and is
                             available from, the jewellery trade.

FIG. 25
A low-cost ceramic saw is ideal for cutting the ceramic elements roughly to size prior to
                               filing the ceramic to fit the burner body.

FIG. 26
Cutting a rectangular piece of ceramic material with a ceramic saw.

FIG. 27
 Carefully held in the vice, sawing a round ceramic element to shape from a square piece of
              sheet. The outline marked in pencil clearly shows where to cut.

   Although it is hard, the ceramic material can be readily cut with a
ceramic saw, such as the one in Figure 25, although the cut edges
can be rather crumbly as they are worked with the saw. Figures 26
and 27 illustrate how to cut rectangular and round pieces of ceramic;

then file or sand them. An old medium file will allow you to trim the
element to the exact size of the burner body.
  Do not over-tighten the vice used to hold the ceramic material. A
slight taper will enable the ceramic element to slide part-way into the
burner body. The ceramic for both burners described in Chapter 5
needs thinning to 9mm (3⁄8 in) by rubbing on sandpaper.





                                      FIG. 28
  A circular piece of the ceramic material cut out ready for installation in a 42mm burner.

   Despite these minor warnings, you should experience no
problems in getting the ceramic to the right shape and size, as can

be seen in Figure 28, but do make regular trial fits in the burner
body.

Ceramic Adhesive

There are several ceramic adhesive fillers available on the market,
but all the burners in this book have been made using white FortaFix
Ceramix TC (Figure 29), except for the two smallest, where Vitcas
Heat Resistant Filler (Figure 30) was used. In addition, Mapei
Mapeflex Firestop (Figure 31) has been used successfully on two
additional burners, and although grey in colour, it also works well. All
three adhesives can withstand temperatures of over 1,000°C, and
they can be obtained from fireplace shops, DIY stores, Amazon and
the Internet.





                                      FIG. 29
 A tube of Ceramix TC high-temperature caulking used to glue the ceramic element, mesh
                       and springs into the metal housing.

FIG. 30
    Vitcas heat-resistant filler for gluing ceramic material and other metal parts inside the
                                          burner.





                                      FIG. 31
  Mapei Mapeflex Firestop high-temperature grout can also be used to glue ceramic and
                                    metal parts.

   These adhesives set fairly quickly, but need to harden for at least
twenty-four hours. Their thickness allows them to fill any small gaps
between the ceramic and its casing. When applied, the adhesive

fillers are water soluble, allowing them to be smoothed and any
excess wiped off. They are also odourless. In addition, they should
be used to secure any mesh or spring, used for gas diffusion, in the
burner casing.
   Ceramix TC is a water-based thixotropic ceramic sealing
compound designed for use where heat resistance is an important
requirement. Vitcas® Heat Resistant Sealant is a high-temperature
sealing and caulking paste. Mapeflex Firestop 1200°C is an
asbestos-free, quick-setting, rigid, silicate refractory fire-resistant
sealing grout. It is used for joining or sealing ceramics to metal. All
three materials provide good adhesion and gap filling to seal and join
these materials, and it should not be difficult to obtain a neat finish
around the ceramic.

Although it is not essential to paint the metal body of completed
burners, they do look better with a painted finish, especially the
copper parts.

reasonably high temperature: those suitable for painting barbecues
are ideal. Most will withstand temperatures up to 600°C and come in
tins or in aerosols. Two popular brands, Blackfriar High-Heat
Resistant Paint and Hammerite Barbecue Paint, are illustrated in
Figure 32, but there are many alternatives. They can be painted or
sprayed directly on to copper. The most widely available colour is
black, usually matt, and a small 125ml or 250ml tin will more than
suffice.

700°C, and it is only too easy to burn yourself. The second reason
for using them is when plugging a lit burner into the flue of a boiler:
once the burner is lit, its bodywork will heat up fairly quickly, and with

GAS FOR SILVER SOLDERING

You will need to use liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) to provide the
heat for silver soldering. LPG is a fossil fuel closely linked to oil, and
is used in many applications including heating. The gas has a
powerful odorant added so that leaks are easily detected from the
smell. It is flammable, and heavier (denser) than air, so it settles and
accumulates in low spots. Serious leaks can present a fire hazard, or
even the risk of an explosion.

FIG. 34
 A 13kg bottle of propane carries enough gas to solder the bodies of hundreds of ceramic
                                        burners.

  LPG under pressure is available in portable cylinders. When
compressed, it readily changes to a liquid, so a large amount of gas
can be stored in a relatively small space. However, in order to be

burned the LPG must be able to boil, expanding significantly to form
a gas. Propane is supplied in a range of cylinder sizes of which
those suitable for use in home workshops contain either 6kg or 13kg
of the liquid gas and will power a torch with a small nozzle for a very
long time. Figure 34 shows a typical cylinder. Propane cylinders
connect to torches through fittings with left-hand threads.





                                      FIG. 35
   A MAP (methylacetylene-propadiene) gas torch screwed on to a MAP gas cylinder.

For silver soldering, propane is the gas normally employed by
model engineers, though MAPP gas – methylacetylene-propadiene
propane – is a useful alternative where relatively small amounts of
heat are required, such as when making ceramic burners. It is also
called MAP gas. It burns at just over 2,000ºC, whereas propane
burns at a little below that figure. The increased temperature and the
design of MAPPgas burners help to simplify silver soldering small
items such as the bodies of ceramic burners. Figure 35 is a photo of
a MAP-gas torch. The cylinders for MAP gas contain a nominal 400g
(14oz) of gas, and although it is at least 50 per cent more expensive
than propane, not much gas is used when making a burner.



  BASIC SAFETY NOTICE

   Most of you will hate ‘health and safety’ warnings, but the best
   advice for all model engineers is to read any warning and
   remember to be careful – as careful as you would be when
   dealing with gas or electricity in your home or petrol in your
    car. You need to observe some safety precautions when using
   propane or MAP gas, which are both forms of LPG, for silver
   soldering.

  ■ LPG is denser than air. Any leaking gases will pool on your
     workshop floor so it is essential to check that your
     connecters and pipework are correctly installed and do not
      leak. You should frequently inspect all of them. In warmer
     weather, you should consider silver soldering in a shady
     outdoor place – though be aware this will make it harder to
     judge when the item you are soldering is coming up to red
     heat

■ Always carefully turn off the gas at the cylinder at the end of
     each soldering session. If you are using a propane torch,
     disconnect the pipes from the gas cylinder once you have
      finished soldering
  ■ Inevitably your gas torch will heat up metal quickly – and
     your skin if you are not careful. So do wear a pair of
      protective gloves when silver soldering. Even with the torch
       off for a couple of minutes, its metal can still burn you
      painfully if you touch it
  ■ Be careful if you use dilute sulphuric acid as a pickle. Never
    add water to acid, only ever add acid to water. Wear
      protective clothes, gloves and a face mask. If you do get
     acid on your skin or clothes, quickly wash it off with water.
    And only dispose of the acid after neutralizing it with baking
     powder

You will need some facilities for silver soldering to make any of the
burners. You may already have some silver solder and flux, as well
as a gas torch. The two practical alternatives are a propane gas
torch and cylinder with a choice of nozzle sizes, or a MAPP gas
torch where the burner head screws on to the top of the small gas
cylinder. The head also contains a piezo-electric ignition system.

they do not require a huge amount of heat to raise their temperature
sufficiently to silver solder them. Thus a propane gas torch (like the
one in Figure 36) is, perhaps, overkill for making ceramic burners –
but such a torch will have many other uses including building steam
boilers to power locomotives, traction engines, lorries or static steam

torches used for soft soldering will not provide sufficient heat for
silver soldering.

SILVER SOLDERING

It is essential to realize that soft solder is unsuitable for making the
burners in this book because it has little or no strength at the
temperatures experienced in a burner body. Even worse, a joint
failure could cause a gas leak, which is also potentially dangerous.
Finally, it is worth remembering that any metal that has been soft
soldered cannot then be silver soldered. For those who have already
built a boiler, silver soldering a burner should provide no problems.
For those who are inexperienced, it is not difficult to become
proficient at silver soldering, and making burners is an ideal place to
start acquiring the techniques. The following are a few important
issues that must be learned:

ISSUE 1: All the parts of the burner that are to be silver soldered
must be completely clean. This means removing any oxides, grease
(including finger marks), oil and dirt. As a minimum, this involves
cleaning well with wire wool until the metal shines. Seriously stained
metal can be pickled and then washed in water to clean it.

preferred, non-cadmium bearing, relatively low-temperature silver

and provides moderate fillets.

the mixture has the consistency of thick cream. Only a small amount

Regardless, silver solder is expensive to buy so take care not to
waste it.

ISSUE 3: A suitable heat source that provides sufficient but not
excessive heat should be used. For building ceramic burners, a
relatively low-cost, self-contained MAPP gas torch, if you have
access to one, is ideal. However, if you already have a propane

from a large propane gas cylinder. And do wear heat-resistant gloves

Sifbronze Brazing

Because silver solder is expensive due to its high silver content,
experiments were made using Sifbronze, a brass (despite its name)
brazing alloy that is much cheaper. It does, however, have a much

higher melting temperature of 875°C–895°C than silver solder, and it
resulted in brass components in the burner melting. It is therefore not
recommended for making ceramic burners. Silver solder is by far the
best solution, and you will not use much.

completed the soldering but before fitting any gas-diffusing
components or the ceramic. This is readily done in a pickle of either
citric or dilute sulphuric acid. Figure 45 shows a burner body after
pickling. However, you must wait until the burner is completely cool
before putting in any pickle.

                     (LPG)


       HIS CHAPTER LOOKS AT the various aspects of using liquefied
      petroleum gas (LPG) to heat ceramic burners. It covers the
      features of the various gases, how best to contain them, andT
which are best suited to heating small steam boilers. Various safety
issues are discussed, and it is important to apply them. Finally, the
chapter also provides information about small gas containers and
refillable tanks.
   As mentioned at the start of Chapter 2, LPG is used in many
applications, including silver soldering. It is also a popular heat
source for small steam boilers. For heating these boilers, the gas is
available as propane, butane, or as a mixture of the two. It has an
unpleasant smell so leaks can be easily detected. LPG burns readily
and is denser than air so it pools in low areas. Any leaks present a
fire risk. While the physical properties of butane and propane are
similar, both gases are poisonous, although butane is less toxic than
propane and can be legally stored indoors.
   The difference in the properties of propane and butane means
that they are particularly suited to specific uses. Propane’s lower
boiling point of –42ºC suits outdoor use. Butane does not work well
in colder conditions, only vaporizing just above –2ºC, and is best
used indoors or outside in the summer months. Otherwise the
performance of the two gases is very similar in terms of flame
temperature and calorific value.

LPG can be compressed into very small cylinders. It changes
easily to a liquid under pressure, so reasonable amounts of gas can
be stored in a relatively small volume. However, to work in a ceramic
burner, the LPG must be able to boil into a gas. Liquid propane
expands 250 times when it turns from a liquid to a gas. When LPG is
released from its pressurized canister, it boils, turns into a gas, and
in doing so cools the liquid in the container. Thus the LPG
temperature will drop some way below ambient, and this can prevent
butane alone from boiling and so producing a useful gas supply,
even when the outside temperature is significantly above freezing.
This can still be a problem with a propane/butane mix when, for
example, sailing a steam-powered boat on a cold, windy day.
   The ceramic burners described in this book are all designed to
run on LPG. Of the various types of LPG, a butane and propane
mixture, typically 70/30, sometimes with isobutane, is the preferred
fuel to be used in ceramic burners suitable for heating model steam
boilers. To provide the gas for the burner either a small disposable
canister can be used, or a refillable gas tank can be fitted, and
loaded with gas from one of the larger disposable cans. Always fill
any refillable tank out of doors so that any inevitable leakage
dissipates safely.
    In northern Europe, especially in the winter months, the best
compromise is the mix of propane and butane commonly found in
the small gas cartridges produced for camping stoves and gas
lamps. This mix is widely available in small- and medium-size
disposable canisters. These canisters can be bought from DIY,
camping and caravan equipment stores.
   Experience has shown that in operation, particularly in cold
weather, gas cylinders can quickly become so cold that their output
pressure and rate of gas flow can fall to the point where insufficient
heat is available from the burner to keep the boiler steaming at the
rate required to drive its engine. For static installations, the solution

is simple: place the gas cylinder in a bowl of warm water, and the
gas flow will almost immediately increase to its normal level. For
installations in boats and land vehicles, the solution is rather harder.
One answer is to feed warm air around the gas tank. An option is to
install a small electric fan to blow warm air into the compartment
containing the gas tank. Another alternative that can help is to run a
copper strip from beneath the boiler’s burner to the gas tank to
conduct heat from one to the other.
   For those who prefer a gas tank integrated into the system,
particularly for model boat use, a number of designs are available
from model engineering suppliers. For those who want a system that
controls the gas flow to the burner as the pressure in the boiler
varies, one of several commercially available solutions can be
purchased, both electronic and mechanical. These are described in
Chapter 8.

  CONTAINER SAFETY TESTING

   At least every five years, safety checks must be carried out on
   any refillable gas tank to check for leaks. Disposable tanks
   are exempt from this requirement. Remove the tank from its
   location in your model, and also remove any covering, but
   leave the gas filler valve and gas control valve in place. The
    test involves filling the tank with your usual LPG, and raising
   the gas mixture to approximately 20ºC to test for leaks from
   the fittings. This is most easily done by immersing the tank in
   a bucket of water at 20ºC and checking for bubbles.
    A soap-bubble test is more sensitive, and involves
   spraying or painting the complete tank with a mix of water,
    liquid soap and glycerine. Bubbles formed by gas escaping
   indicate a leak. This test can be carried out with cladding on
   the tank. Any observable leak is regarded as a failure, and the
   tank and fittings must be repaired and then re-submitted for a
    further safeguard test. However, a slow leak from the gas

valve to the gas jet is not a reason for failure, but requires a
valve change.

Burner Blowback

On any of the burners that fit under boilers, rather than fit into
horizontal flues, burner blowback is indicated by a sudden roaring
noise. This means that the flame is now also burning beneath the
ceramic, and it will rapidly damage and then destroy parts of the
burner. Immediately turn off the gas and allow the burner to cool

with burners that plug into flues.)

normally too much primary air. To avoid blowback, always set the
gas-jet holder further in than the optimum, and then carefully and
slowly move it further out to get the best possible blue flame. If you
have experienced blowback, before attempting to relight the burner,
make sure that the gas-jet holder is moved a little further into its
housing. After relighting the burner, recheck the flame and readjust
the position of the gas jet in the housing until it is burning correctly.

Boiler Howling

Any horizontal boiler with a flue, into which the burner is plugged,
has the potential to howl. The problem is caused by the acoustic
characteristics of the flue and chimney/funnel combination. Its
length, any obstructions such as Galloway tubes, super heater or
bends, can interact with the velocity of gas and air flow through the
flue. It may also be altered by changes in atmospheric conditions
such as humidity, pressure and temperature. While howling is not an

uncommon problem, it is relatively straightforward to solve by trial
and error.
   You can try increasing the size of the gas jet and reducing the
flow at the gas valve. These two measures should enable you to set
the blue cones on the burner, but with the speed of the gas coming
out of the jet reduced. Increasing the gas jet one or two sizes should
quickly resolve the problem without altering the heat output of the
burner. It is a simple question of balancing the variables, jet size, the
amount the gas valve is open, and the associated air flow and the
amount of noise from the flue. However, do warm up the flue first at
a low gas setting before any work to eliminate howling is carried out.

BURNER INSTALLATION

After setting up the burner correctly, turn off the gas so the burner
can cool before installing it in the firebox of the boiler or plugging it
into the flue. It is essential that plenty of fresh secondary air can
enter the flue or firebox. Only the smallest 28mm burners have
secondary air holes bored in their outer casings – the other flue-
mounted burners obtain sufficient secondary air through the gas-jet
housing.
   The larger burners and the two smallest flatbottomed ones sit in
the fireboxes of their boilers. It is important to ensure that these
fireboxes have ample air holes. Too much air is not a problem, but
too little will inhibit effective burning, will reduce heat output, and in
severe cases, can cause damage to the burner.

PIPEWORK AND VALVES

When connecting a gas source to a boiler burner take care that the
joints are all gas tight. It is sensible to apply soapy water to each
joint and to ensure that when the gas is on, it is not blowing any
bubbles. A manual gas valve that is screwed on to a disposable gas
tank, or a similar valve fitted to a refillable gas tank, controls the gas
flow. Normally 1⁄8in outsidediameter copper pipe should be used to
connect the gas to the burner. One end usually terminates in a
manual screw fitting that goes on to the gas valve; the other joins to
the gas jet holder. However, sometimes you will need to use 1⁄4mm ×
40ME coned connectors.

When installing gas jets and connecting up gas pipework, the use of
a gas sealant is recommended to make the joints gas tight. Loctite
542, Heldite or Rocol pipe-jointing compound are all suitable and
only need smearing on the joints to provide a gas-tight seal. They
are available from plumbers’ merchants and DIY stores.

   Any ceramic burner requires a gas tank to hold its fuel, but some
sort of gas-control system will also be needed. This may be just a
simple on/off valve that is built into, or screws on to the gas tank,
with a pipe that runs to the gas jet in the burner (see Figure 193).
Such a valve can be used, partly open, to set the rate of gas flow

manually. This can only be done by looking at the burner, although
this can be difficult in some installations. For running a static steam
engine and boiler combination in the workshop, this is usually an
adequate approach. However, it is less than satisfactory in a mobile
application such as a steam launch or a small steam lorry. Thus your
chosen solution may also be a more complex one that senses boiler
pressure and varies the gas flow to the burner in order to maintain
the required pressure.
   The type and size of gas tank depends both on individual choice
and on the environment in which the burner is intended to be used.
For a static application, a disposable gas-can with a simple gas
valve can be fitted; the valve can then be manually operated to
increase or decrease the gas flow to the burner and thus maintain
pressure in the boiler as the engine consumes steam. Equally a
refillable gas tank with a similar gas valve can be fitted.
    In both cases, if the safety valve starts to lift with the engine
running, it is a simple matter to turn down the gas flow so that the
ceramic burner provides rather less heat to the boiler. Similarly the
gas flow can be turned up if the boiler pressure starts to fall. All this
assumes that the boiler and engine are a good match.
   For marine applications and for small-scale steam lorries and
traction engines, as well as small-gauge locomotives and other
mobile applications, it is essential that the gas supply is exhausted
before all the water in the boiler has been used. This implies fitting a
relatively small gas tank to supply the burner. Its size depends on the
water capacity of the boiler it heats, whether a boiler feed pump is
fitted to the engine, and the volume of its water supply as well as the
size of the engine, its steam consumption, and the way it is
operated. An oscillating engine will always have a significantly higher
steam consumption than a side-valve one and will require more heat
from the burner, all other things being equal.

Do you plan to run your engine mostly at full power, or much of
the time well throttled back, or even at times stationary? Think about
these variables carefully and decide the size of the gas tank
accordingly.
   Having chosen the gas tank, a connector and valve will be
needed regardless of whether a boiler pressure-control system is
fitted as well. The decision to install one is often price dependent, as
a complex gas-control installation is not cheap.

AUTOMATIC BOILER CONTROL

There are several commercial solutions that aim to provide a
constant boiler steam pressure regardless of steam consumption.
There are both electronic and mechanical systems that fit between
the boiler and the gas tank. An electronic gas valve automatically
controls gas flow to the burner using a pressure sensor fitted to the
boiler. It reduces the gas flow to just a pilot when the pressure is
sufficient. The chosen pressure can be set with a screwdriver
adjustment on the electronic control box. However, a servo will have
to be provided in order to move the gas valve, although this servo
will not be connected to, and will operate independently from, any
radiocontrol system that may be fitted.
   The alternative mechanical solutions use a flexible membrane,
connected to boiler pressure, to control the flow of gas. The required
pressure is set using a simple screw adjustment. The advantages
and disadvantages of the two different types of system and their cost
are likely to affect your choice. When looking at electronic systems,
remember there will be a battery to charge or replace, and the cost
of the extra servo. Balanced against this are the simpler controls that
you may find are easier to adjust on electronic solutions.

ELECTRONIC SYSTEMS

Using a pressure sensor fitted to the boiler and a battery-powered
electronic control box, a servo (independent of any radio-control
system) automatically adjusts gas flow to the burner via a servo-
operated gas valve. The movement of the valve reduces the gas flow
to just a pilot when the pressure is sufficient, and increases it again
when the pressure falls. The chosen pressure can be set with a
screw adjustment on the electronic control box.

thumb-wheel adjustment on the regulator valve. Figure 199 shows

reached, the regulator reduces gas flow to a pilot and vice-versa

   The maker or owner/user must ensure that the tank is only used
with butane or a butane/propane mix below 40 per cent propane,
and never exceeds a temperature of 60ºC. Every tank shall be
indelibly marked with a unique identification number. The form and
position of the marking shall not damage or compromise the
structure of the tank. The tank shall also carry a mark indicating the
type of LPG for which it was constructed.

THE ROLE OF INSPECTORS

Inspectors are appointed by the associations, and may test a tank
only if its maker or current owner/ user is a member of the
associations. Inspectors undertake their duties on a voluntary non-
commercial basis, and all examinations and tests are carried out
entirely at their discretion. Inspectors will only test and certify a tank
that they feel competent to test, based on their own experience. A
test certificate will be issued only by an inspector. Inspectors shall
not inspect their own work, unless that work has already been tested
and passed by another inspector.

HYDRAULIC TEST

The tank should be without fittings, and unmounted in order that it
may be inspected all round. If this is impractical, the agreement of
the inspector will be required before the test can proceed. This
requirement applies to both initial and any subsequent hydraulic
tests.
   The specified initial test pressure for the hydraulic test of the
tank, as described in this code, shall be 400psi gauge pressure. This
will apply for all tanks, regardless of whether they are intended to be
used for butane only, or a butane/propane mix with a maximum
propane content of 40 per cent. The test gauge range should be
approximately 1.5 times the pressure of the test (for example, a
range 0–600psi will be satisfactory for test pressures up to 400psi),
and within the previous two years should have been checked and
calibrated to within ±2 per cent, either against a currently validated
dead-weight test apparatus or against other traceable equipment.
The test gauge may also be calibrated by a commercial test facility,
which will provide a calibration test certificate.

The tank shall be indelibly marked with a unique identification
number. The form and position of the marking shall not damage or
compromise the structure of the tank. The tank shall also carry a
mark indicating the type of LPG for which it was constructed.
   The procedure shall consist of raising the hydraulic pressure from
zero to the test pressure, stopping at several intermediate pressures
for careful visual examination until the full test pressure is attained.
Each test pressure shall be held long enough to investigate any
distortion of the vessel, and to confirm that any fall in pressure is not
caused by structural weakness, and that there are no observable
leaks.

SAFEGUARD TEST

The tank should be unmounted but with the gas filler valve and gas
control valve in place. The tank shall be filled with LPG of a type
specified by the maker or owner/user, and the gas mixture should be
at, or raised to approximately 20ºC to test for leaks from the fittings.
Any observable leak shall be regarded as a failure, and the tank and
fittings shall be repaired and then resubmitted for a further safeguard
test.
    After completion of the hydraulic and safeguard tests, safety
checks shall be carried out on the gas tank at no longer than five-
year intervals, or when the model is next used if greater than that
time interval since previous use.

SAFETY CHECK

A safety check shall be conducted at five-yearly intervals. It shall
take the form of a leak test.

Where reasonably practicable the whole of the tank shall be
examined visually by removal of any covering. Where this is not
possible, the accessible tank joints and unions should be sprayed or
covered with soap solution to reveal any leakage.
   Any leakage observed must be corrected before any further use
of the tank.

CERTIFICATES

The certificate used as part of this code will be given to the
owner/user of the tank for safekeeping, and will be common across,
and available from the associations. Each certificate shall bear the
following information:

■ The name of the club/society and organization issuing the
   certificate
■ The name of the owner/user
■ The location where the test was carried out
■ Identification of the system that the certificate relates to, for
  example the boiler number
■ The maker of the tank
■ The tank identification markings
■ Material(s) used in construction
■ Date of construction, if known
■ Test pressure of the test just completed
■ Signatures of the inspector and the witness
■ Notes and comments where applicable
